# Teach the agent your project {#sec-teach}

Open a real analysis folder, one you've worked in for a few months, and look at it as
a stranger would. There's a `data/` folder, but is everything in it raw, or did someone
save a filtered table there too? There are four scripts with names like `qc.R`,
`qc_v2.R` and `qc_final_SD.R`: which one is current? A `results/` folder holds figures
from last spring, and nothing says whether they came from the current script. The
sample sheet has a column called `cond`, and only you know that `1` is the knockout.

An agent opening that folder is the stranger. It reads quickly and well: files, code,
headers, any README it finds. What it can't read is **what's only in your head**. Which
files it must never touch. Where new output goes. The convention that looks like a
mistake and isn't. What "done" means to you. So it guesses, reasonably, and some of its
guesses are wrong *for you*. You correct it. Next session it has forgotten, and you
correct it again.

This morning's talk made the fix sound simple: write it down once, in a file the agent
reads at the start of every session. It is simple, but there are two traps. The first is
writing too much: a long file that restates what the agent could have read for itself,
which costs context on every turn and buries the few lines that matter. The second is
copying: pasting the sample-sheet description into the agent's file as well as the
README, so there are now two versions to keep in step, and one of them will drift.

This chapter is about writing the short file, and pointing to everything else.

## What you'll learn

- The difference between a **README**, which is for people, and an **AGENTS.md** (or
  `CLAUDE.md`), which is for agents.
- How Claude Code finds and loads these files, and how to make one file work for
  several tools.
- How to **link** to other documents instead of copying them, and when an `@` import is
  the better choice.
- A loop for finding what belongs in the file: explore, correct, write it down, test it
  in a fresh session.

## Two files, two readers

Most projects that have any documentation have a README. It's written for a person:
someone new to the lab, a collaborator, a reviewer, you in a year. It says what the
project is, how to run it and who to ask. It can be friendly and discursive, because
people skim.

An `AGENTS.md` is written for an agent, and it should contain **only what an agent can't
work out by reading the folder**, written as rules. The agent will read your README and
your code anyway; the agent's file doesn't need to explain them. What it needs are the
things no amount of reading would reveal: *`data/` is read-only*, *new output goes in
`results/`*, *check the direction of a fold change before you state it*. Write those as
**must** and **must not**. "We generally prefer" reads as advice to a person and as
negotiable to an agent.

| | README.md | AGENTS.md |
|---|---|---|
| **Written for** | People: newcomers, collaborators, reviewers, you later | Coding agents |
| **Says** | What this is, how to run it, where the data came from, who to ask | Only what an agent can't discover: rules, boundaries, what "done" means |
| **Tone** | Explanatory, friendly | Imperative: *must*, *must not* |
| **Length** | As long as it needs to be | Short. Under a page; every line costs context, every session |
| **When it's read** | When someone opens it | Loaded automatically at the start of each session |
| **Goes wrong when** | Nobody writes it | It restates the README, or goes out of date and keeps giving orders |

: A README and an AGENTS.md do different jobs. The agent reads both, but only one is
loaded into every session. {#tbl-teach-readme-vs-agents}

::: {.column-margin}
**Same idea, different names.** `AGENTS.md` is an open convention that many tools read
[@url:https://agents.md]. Claude Code's own name is `CLAUDE.md`. Google Antigravity
reads `AGENTS.md` (and `GEMINI.md`), and so does Codex. Check your tool's documentation if
you're not on Claude Code.
:::

A good README helps the agent too. It's often the first file an agent opens, and in the
worked example below it did most of the work [@doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006561]. The
advice for organising a computational project hasn't changed because agents arrived:
keep raw data separate from results, record what you did, and make it possible for
someone else to follow [@doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510;
@doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000424]. Agents are simply the most literal "someone else"
you'll ever have.

### How Claude Code finds the file

Claude Code reads its instructions at the start of every session
[@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory]. The details matter, because a file in
the wrong place, or with the wrong name, is silently ignored.

- **`CLAUDE.md`** in the folder you start the session in, and in every folder above it,
  is loaded at launch. All of them are concatenated; none overrides another.
- **`AGENTS.md`** is read *instead*, but only when there's no `CLAUDE.md` in the folder
  or above it. This needs a recent version of Claude Code (2.1.277 or later), and the
  documentation notes it isn't read in the **first session after you install or
  upgrade**, which is exactly the situation many people are in today.
- **Files in subfolders** (`data/CLAUDE.md`, say) aren't loaded at launch. They're read
  when the agent opens a file in that folder.

The simplest arrangement that works everywhere is two files: write your rules in
`AGENTS.md`, which every tool can read, and add a `CLAUDE.md` containing one line:

```default
@AGENTS.md
```

That line is an **import**. Claude Code expands it, so `CLAUDE.md` loads the whole of
`AGENTS.md`, whatever version you're on. Other tools ignore `CLAUDE.md` and read
`AGENTS.md` directly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Did it load?

In the `claude` command-line tool, type `/context`: your instruction files are listed
under memory files. In any tool, you can start a session and ask *"What instructions
did you load for this folder?"*, then compare the answer with the file. If it doesn't
mention your rules, check the file's name and location before anything else.
:::

## Link, don't copy

Your project probably already has documents an agent would find useful: a description
of the sample sheet, a protocol, notes on how the data were processed. The tempting move
is to paste them into `AGENTS.md`. Don't. **Point to them instead.**

```markdown
The sample sheet's columns are described in [docs/samples.md](docs/samples.md).
What each data file is, and its known quirks: [data/README.md](data/README.md).
```

A link does three things. The agent's file stays short. The document stays in one
place, so there's one version to keep current. And the agent reads it **when it needs
it**: working on the sample sheet, it follows the link; fixing a plotting script, it
doesn't.

Claude Code also has the import you've just seen: `@docs/samples.md`, outside
backticks, pulls the whole file into every session at launch, the way `@AGENTS.md` does.

| | Markdown link | `@` import (Claude Code) |
|---|---|---|
| **Written as** | `[docs/samples.md](docs/samples.md)` | `@docs/samples.md` |
| **Loaded** | When the agent decides it needs it | At the start of every session |
| **Costs context** | Only when read | Always |
| **Other tools** | Understood everywhere | Only Claude Code; others see plain text |
| **Use for** | Almost everything | The few documents every session needs, such as `@AGENTS.md` |

: Links are read when needed; imports are always loaded. {#tbl-teach-link-vs-import}

@fig-teach-folder shows the arrangement: a README for people, a short `AGENTS.md` for
agents that links to the detailed documents, and a one-line `CLAUDE.md` that imports it.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-teach-folder
%%| fig-cap: "A project folder that teaches its agent. Solid arrows: loaded at the start
%%|   of every session. Dashed arrows: links the agent follows when it needs them."
%%| fig-alt: "Diagram. CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md, which is loaded every session.
%%|   AGENTS.md links to data/README.md and docs/samples.md, read when needed, and
%%|   sets rules for data/, scripts/ and results/. README.md is for people."
flowchart LR
  accDescr: Diagram. CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md, which is loaded every session.
  C["CLAUDE.md<br/>(one line: @AGENTS.md)"] ==>|import| A["AGENTS.md<br/>rules for agents"]
  R["README.md<br/>for people"]
  A -.->|link| DR["data/README.md<br/>what each file is"]
  A -.->|link| S["docs/samples.md<br/>sample sheet"]

  A -->|"new output here"| O[("results/")]
  A -->|"current code"| SC[("scripts/")]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## `/init`, and why it's only a start

Claude Code's `/init` command writes a starting `CLAUDE.md` by analysing the folder: the
commands, layout and conventions it discovers. That's useful in a large codebase, but
notice what it can't include: anything that isn't discoverable. Treat what it writes
as a draft, delete what the agent could have read for itself, and add the rules only
you know.
:::

## Worked example

We tried this on the fallback data you'll meet below: the Vahedi lab's teaching files,
arranged as a small analysis project with a `data/` folder (DESeq2 tables, a counts
matrix, a messy sample sheet and the data README) and a `scripts/` folder holding one
QC script, which is broken on purpose. We used Claude Code 2.1.280 with Claude Opus 5.5,
from the command line, on 23 September 2026, with no personal instructions loaded. Your
run will word things differently. The outputs below are real, lightly trimmed.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-teach-loop
%%| fig-cap: "The loop in this chapter. The file is written from your corrections, not
%%|   from a description of the project."
%%| fig-alt: "Cycle: explore and summarise, then correct what it got wrong, then write
%%|   AGENTS.md from the corrections, then test in a new session, then back to
%%|   correcting."
flowchart LR
  accDescr: Cycle - explore and summarise, then correct what it got wrong, then write
  E["1. Explore<br/>and summarise"] --> K["2. Correct<br/>what it got wrong"]
  K --> W["3. Write AGENTS.md<br/>from the corrections"]
  W --> T["4. New session:<br/>does it hold?"]
  T -->|"something slipped"| K
```

**1. Explore.** We asked for a summary, and nothing else:

```default
Explore this folder and summarise it for me in under 250 words: what each file is,
which are raw data and which are results, what analysis this is, and anything you'd
need to ask me before doing further work here. Don't change any files.
```

It took about 20 seconds. The summary was good, because the data README is good: it
had both experiments right, noticed that the two DESeq2 tables have **fold changes
pointing in opposite directions**, and found three of the script's bugs by reading it.
Its questions were the useful part:

> 1. The README lists `scbasecount_paper.pdf` and a `tools/` folder, but neither is
>    here. Are they missing, or not needed?
> 2. What's the goal: fixing the script, cleaning the sample sheet, or new analysis?
> 4. May I write output files, and where? The data can't be redistributed outside the
>    workshop.

Every one of those is something it couldn't have found by reading. That's the list to
work from.

**2. Correct, and 3. write it down.** We answered its questions and added two things
we'd have had to say sooner or later, then asked it to turn the lot into rules:

```default
You explored this folder a moment ago. Here is what you got wrong or had to ask,
and my answers:

- The paper and tools/ folder aren't needed; ignore them.
- Everything in data/ is read-only. Never edit, overwrite or move those files.
  New output goes in results/, which you can create.
- The goal changes from task to task; I'll say each time.
- Before you state which way a fold change points, check it against the counts,
  not just the README.
- These data are not to leave this computer: don't upload them or paste them
  anywhere.
- "Done" means a file in results/ and one line saying how you checked it.

Write an AGENTS.md in this folder that captures just those, as rules (must / must
not) for a future session. Keep it under 20 lines. Don't repeat what data/README.md
already says: link to it instead. Also write a one-line CLAUDE.md containing only
@AGENTS.md. Then show me both files.
```

It wrote this `AGENTS.md`, fourteen lines, and a `CLAUDE.md` holding only `@AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
# Rules for this folder

What the data files are: see [data/README.md](data/README.md). Don't restate it; read it.

- You must not use the paper or `tools/`. They are not needed.
- You must not edit, overwrite, move or delete anything in `data/`. Treat it as read-only.
- You must write all new output to `results/`. Create it if it doesn't exist.
- You must not assume a standing goal. The user states the goal for each task.
- You must check fold-change direction against the raw counts before you state it.
  The README alone is not enough.
- You must not upload these data or paste them into any external service, website or tool.
  They stay on this computer.
- A task is done only when there is a file in `results/` and you give one line
  saying how you checked it.
```

Read it the way you'd read a colleague's protocol. It linked to the data README rather
than copying it, as asked. Two lines deserve editing. "Must not use the paper" has
turned *it isn't here* into a prohibition; harmless, but not what we meant. "Must not
assume a standing goal" is true of every session and earns nothing; we'd delete it.
**The agent writes the file; you edit it.**

**4. Test it in a new session.** A fresh session, a real task, and none of the rules
repeated:

```default
Fix scripts/make_qc_report.py so it gives correct answers, run it on the peak table,
and tell me how many peaks are gained and lost in the knockout at padj < 0.05 and
|log2FC| > 1.
```

It fixed six bugs, changed the script to write its report and plot into `results/`, and
gave the right numbers: **2,202 gained, 3,056 lost**, matching the data README and an
independent count we made with `awk`. The data files were untouched (we compared
checksums). It ended with the line the rules asked for, saying how it had checked.

And it did something we hadn't expected. The fold-change rule says to check direction
against the counts, but **the peak table has no counts**. So it said so:

> The project rules say to check it against raw counts, but the peak table has none.
> The "gained/lost" labels therefore rely on `data/README.md`.

That's a rule written from one file's lesson (the gene table, whose direction is the
surprising one) meeting a file it doesn't fit. It's a better outcome than silent
compliance, and a sign the rule needs rewording: *where the table has count columns,
check…*.

**Did the file make a difference?** We ran the same task in an identical folder with no
`AGENTS.md`. That run also fixed the bugs and got 2,202 and 3,056, and it didn't touch
the data either. The differences were narrower than you might expect: without the file,
the script still wrote its plot into whichever folder it was run from, and the answer
stated the direction from the README without saying it was unchecked. **Most of the
work was done by a good data README.** The agent's file added the few rules about *how
we work*, and that's all it should do.

::: {.column-margin}
Both runs also found that this computer's Python had no `pandas`, and neither could
install it without permission. Each wrote an independent check with Python's built-in
`csv` module instead, and said so. We ran the fixed script afterwards, with `pandas`
supplied by `uv`, and it printed the same counts.
:::

## Your turn

About 30 minutes. You need a folder with some history: **several scripts, some data,
some results**. A single notebook is too simple to show much.

::: {.callout-important}
## Privacy: work on a copy

The agent will read every file in the folder. Use data you're allowed to share with the
tool you're using: nothing identifiable, no patient data, nothing unpublished you
haven't been cleared to use this way. If the folder matters, **work on a copy** until
you trust your rules.
:::

**Your own folder.** Start a new session with the analysis folder as its project folder,
and check with *"What folder are you in?"*

**The fallback.** Inside `Documents/agents-workshop/`, make an empty folder called
`teach-demo`, start a new session there ([Setup](00-setup.qmd)), and paste this:

```default
In this folder, make two subfolders, data and scripts. Download these files from
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/main/track-a/data/
into data/: README.md, differential_peaks.csv, differential_genes.tsv,
counts_matrix.csv and sample_sheet_messy.csv. Download make_qc_report.py from the
same place into scripts/. Save each file exactly as downloaded, with curl (or
Invoke-WebRequest on Windows); don't retype or rewrite any of them. Don't clone the
repository. Then list what you downloaded with each file's size.
```

That's about 11.5 MB: the peak table is 6.7 MB, the gene table 3.5 MB, the counts
1.3 MB, and the rest a few KB each. These are real data from the Vahedi lab, shared for
the workshop: don't redistribute them.

Now work through the loop in @fig-teach-loop.

1. **Explore.** Paste the explore prompt from the worked example. Read the summary
   carefully, and keep a list: everything it got wrong, every question it asked, and
   everything you'd have told a new student on their first day.
2. **Sort the list.** Not everything belongs in the agent's file. Use
   @tbl-teach-where-it-goes.
3. **Write it down.** Give the agent your list, using the worked example's second
   prompt as a model. If there's no README, ask for one too, for people: what this is,
   how to run it, who to ask.
4. **Edit what it wrote.** Delete any line the agent could have worked out by reading.
   Reword any rule that's stricter or vaguer than you meant.
5. **Test it.** Start a **new session** in the same folder ([Setup](00-setup.qmd)): it
   begins with an empty conversation and reloads the instruction files. Give it a
   real next task, without repeating any rule. Watch whether the rules hold.
6. **Ledger it.** One entry: what you had to tell it, and whether writing it down
   stopped you having to (@sec-ledger).

| If the correction is… | It goes in… |
|---|---|
| A rule about how to work here: what not to touch, where output goes, what "done" means | `AGENTS.md` |
| A fact about the project a person would need too: what the data are, how to run it | `README.md`, or a doc the README links to |
| A detail of one file, such as the sample sheet's columns | A document next to it, **linked** from `AGENTS.md` |
| Something the agent got wrong once and could have read | Nowhere. Say it in the chat. |

: Where each correction belongs. {#tbl-teach-where-it-goes}

**On Windows:** turn on file name extensions, or a file you save in Notepad may really be
`AGENTS.md.txt`; names starting with a dot (a `.claude` folder) are hidden in File
Explorer by default. See @sec-windows. And don't make `CLAUDE.md` a symbolic link to
`AGENTS.md`, a trick you may see online: on Windows it needs extra rights and can arrive
as a one-line text file. The `@AGENTS.md` import works everywhere.

## What to notice

- **What it asked you.** The questions in the first summary are the best guide to what
  belongs in the file. It asks about what it can't see.
- **How much it got right.** If your folder has a good README, the agent's file can be
  very short. If it got a lot wrong, ask whether the README should say more, for people
  as well as agents.
- **How it rewrote your rules.** Agents turn "ignore X" into "must not use X" and
  soften "never" into "try not to". Your wording is the rule; check it survived.
- **A rule that doesn't fit.** In the worked example, a sensible rule met a file it
  couldn't apply to. When the agent says a rule can't be followed, that's the rule
  telling you to rewrite it.
- **What it did without being told.** A fresh session that behaves well with no file is
  a result too. If your list is empty, write no file.

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-tip}
## You're done when

- [ ] In a new session, *"What rules apply in this folder?"* gets an answer that
      matches your file, and nothing more.
- [ ] Every line in `AGENTS.md` is something the agent couldn't have discovered by
      reading.
- [ ] Nothing appears in both the README and `AGENTS.md`; where it did, one is now a
      link.
- [ ] The new session followed the rules without you repeating them. (If one slipped:
      was the rule unclear, or wasn't the file loaded?)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Instruction files go stale

Conventions change and the file doesn't. Six months on it's confidently telling your
agent to do something you stopped doing in March. Keep it short enough to reread, and
reread it when the project changes, the way you'd review a protocol.
:::

## Going further

- **Rules for one part of a project.** A `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` inside a subfolder
  is read when the agent works there, so `data/AGENTS.md` can hold rules about the
  data alone. Claude Code also has path-scoped rules in `.claude/rules/`
  [@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory].
- **A procedure, not a rule.** If what you're writing down is a multi-step procedure,
  such as how your lab triages a DESeq2 table, it's a skill, not a rule: that's
  @sec-skills.
- **A whole lab's conventions.** The Vahedi lab's afternoon material has a pod that goes
  further, writing the lab's shared definitions (genome build, what counts as a
  promoter, what counts as differential) into one file and showing how differently
  agents answer without it: [Pod 1, Teach the agent your
  lab](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/blob/main/track-b/pod-1-teach-the-agent-your-lab.md).
